title: The Drawer Audit. Counting What the Tools Actually Earned
body: There is a drawer in most homes that works like a museum of good intentions. Mine held three screwdrivers that do the same job, a laser level that came out once, and a bag of fasteners I cannot identify. The audit started as a joke and turned into one of the more useful hours I have spent, because the drawer was not really holding tools. It was holding guesses. The method was embarrassingly simple. Every item came out and got one of three marks. Used this year, used someday, used never. The counts were humbling. Out of twenty six items, seven had earned their place. Seven. The other nineteen were insurance policies against problems that never arrived, bought at full price and stored at full drawer space. Here is the arithmetic that changed how I buy. A tool that gets used weekly earns its spot even if it is cheap and ugly. A tool used once a year is a rental, whether you admit it or not. Divide the price by the number of uses and the true cost appears. The laser level worked out to more per use than hiring the job done. The cheap utility knife worked out to nearly nothing across hundreds of openings. The price tag tells you what you pay at the register; the use count tells you what you actually paid. The second pass was harder, because it meant admitting which purchases were fantasy purchases. The fancy multimeter was a fantasy about being someone who troubleshoots circuits. The carving set was a fantasy about weekends that do not exist. Selling or gifting those stung for a day and then, honestly, it felt like putting something down that was heavy. What stayed tells its own story. A tape measure, two screwdrivers with different tips, a utility knife, pliers, a level that is just a bubble in plastic, and one adjustable wrench. Every fix this year, and there were many, ran through those eight. The jobs did not know the difference. The jobs only needed the right question and one tool that works. The drawer audit now happens once a season, and the rule for new entries is written on a card taped inside. Name the job, name the last time you needed it, or do not bring it home. Tools are not trophies. They are employees, and every employee should be able to point at the work they did this quarter. Count your own drawer sometime this week. What percentage of it actually worked for a living this year?
